then.text: That'll stand a hundred years. Mind you, the keepers built it to keep people off. I'm mending it so you can see over it.
The keepers' wall's come down at the gate. No mortar, no nonsense: stones by size and shape, and gravity does the rest.

else.text: Not my moor to touch until it's someone's to mend. Whose is it, you wonder? Not mine.

then.text: Go on. Walk it. I haven't the heart. I have a pension, and a pension is a very short fence.
This is a private moor, and I'll thank you to take your boots elsewhere.
Oh. You bought it. From the Enclosure's receiver. That is... well. I still draw my wages from the old shoot.

else.text: Keep out. These are the Enclosure's moors, and the grouse are spoken for.

then.text: Hare, curlew, golden plover. All of them back. The sphagnum's holding the water. You did that.
Seven curlew pairs, and a merlin. Good for a moor that was heather and nothing else five years ago.
A mountain hare! Look at the ears on it. The only wild ones in England live on these moors, and now the moor has you.

else.text: Bring me a mountain hare and I'll sign the survey. The only wild ones in England live on the Peak moors. They go white in winter.
I count curlews. Bring a mountain hare some day and I'll count that too.

then.text: Shh. Don't tell the keepers. We start at first light, you know.
Dawn on the High Moor. The mist is lifting off the heather, and a curlew is going up the hill ahead of you.
There you are. I'd hoped someone would come. We were four hundred, and now I'm only one. Keep the gate open for us, would you?
A hundred voices, faint over the ridge, are singing. Then there's only the wind in the heather, and nobody there at all.

else.text: Not yet. We start at first light, and the keepers are still about. Come back at dawn.
Morning. I'm not meant to be here yet. Come back when the moor's alive.

then.text: Look at them go. Three prams, a spaniel and a man in a kilt. Nobody has asked them for a ticket.
Walk it again some time. It's yours. It's everybody's.

else.text: Here it is. The path's on the Definitive Map, in ink, and the gate won't be shut. A right of way, in perpetuity.
There were four hundred of them in 1932. I'd like to think they'd have enjoyed the morning.
Here. Take these boots. They were my father's, and they have walked every moor in the Peak. Wear them out.

arc_england_walker.text: Public footpath, it says. Public! I've been looking at this moor from the road for forty years.
I read the sign twice, just to be sure. Then I walked past it.
